title: Meiosis and sexual reproduction
note: Meiosis is two divisions after one round of DNA replication, turning one diploid cell into four genetically different haploid cells. Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes; meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Crossing over and independent assortment shuffle alleles, and fertilization restores the diploid number.

read.title: Why no two siblings are alike
text: Every human body cell carries 46 chromosomes, 23 inherited from each parent. To make eggs or sperm, the body must cut that number in half, or the count would double each generation. Meiosis does this.

Before meiosis begins, the DNA is copied, so each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids. In prophase I, each chromosome finds its homolog, the matching chromosome from the other parent, and the two pair tightly. While paired, non-sister chromatids trade matching segments. This crossing over creates chromosomes that mix maternal and paternal alleles.

At metaphase I the pairs line up at the center of the cell. Which side the maternal or paternal member faces is random and independent for each pair. With 23 pairs, a single person can produce about 8 million chromosome combinations, before crossing over is even counted. Anaphase I then pulls the homologs apart, halving the number of chromosome sets.

Meiosis II looks like mitosis: sister chromatids separate, leaving four haploid cells. Because of crossing over, independent assortment, and the random meeting of egg and sperm, siblings from the same parents are almost never genetically identical, unless they are identical twins from one zygote.
